title: Embeddings and RAG
summary: How to let a model answer from your own data: turn text into embeddings, search by meaning with pgvector, and feed only the best matches into the prompt.
youWillLearn: What an embedding is, and why it finds meaning that keyword search misses
The two halves of RAG: indexing your data, then retrieving for each question
How to store and search vectors in Supabase with pgvector
The bugs that leak data or serve stale answers, and how to check for them

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.database: A program built to store data safely and find it again fast. Notely's is Postgres, run by Supabase.
glossary.Claude API: Anthropic's AI, reached over the internet: you send it text, it sends text back. Each call costs a little money.
glossary.context window: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can look at in one request.
glossary.embedding: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning get similar lists.
glossary.vector: A list of numbers, like a point on a map with many directions. Embeddings are vectors.
glossary.embedding model: A model whose only job is turning text into an embedding. It is separate from the chat model and much cheaper.
glossary.chunk: A small piece of a longer document, such as a paragraph, embedded and searched on its own.
glossary.RAG: Retrieval-augmented generation: find the most relevant pieces of your own data, put them in the prompt, then let the model answer from them.
glossary.pgvector: A Postgres extension that adds a vector column type and fast nearest-match search. Supabase supports it.
glossary.cosine distance: A way to measure how far apart two vectors point. Smaller distance means closer meaning.
glossary.HNSW: A type of index for vectors that finds near matches very fast by skipping most rows, at the price of being approximate.
glossary.hybrid search: Combining keyword search and vector search, so exact words and similar meanings both count.
glossary.RLS: Row Level Security: Postgres rules that decide which rows each logged-in user may read, enforced by the database itself.

steps.title: Notely's chat searches by keyword
body: Maya has 2,000 notes in Notely, our notes app. They live in the database. When she asks Notely's chat something, the app server (the computer running Notely's code) searches her notes for the words she typed.
The match goes to the Claude API, Anthropic's AI, which answers. Ask about "groceries": it finds the grocery note.

scene.caption: Question in, keyword search in the database, answer from Claude.

steps.title: "What did I decide about the logo?"
body: Maya asks about the logo. The note that answers it says "going with the blue brand mark". It never uses the word logo, so keyword search finds nothing.
Sending all 2,000 notes instead would overflow the context window (the most the model can read at once) and cost a fortune on every question.
changes: ~ Useful matches 1 → 0
~ Database: no note contains the word "logo"

scene.caption: The answer is in the database, but no note uses the word Maya typed.

steps.title: Turn meaning into coordinates
body: An embedding model turns text into an embedding: a vector, a long list of numbers. Think of it as a position on a map of meaning.
Similar texts land near each other, even with no words in common. "Logo decision" and "blue brand mark" sit close; "grocery list" sits far away. Search becomes: find the nearest points.

callout.text: A library shelved by topic, not by title. Walk to where your question would sit, and the useful books are right there, whatever their titles say.

changes: − Maya, App Server, Claude API, Database: we zoom into meaning
+ Question, Brand Mark, Font List: close together
+ Groceries and Gym Plan: far away

scene.caption: On the map of meaning, Maya's question lands right next to the brand mark note.

steps.title: Step 1: index the notes once
body: Ahead of time, the app server splits each note into chunks of a paragraph or so, sends each to an embedding model, and stores the vector next to its text, using pgvector (a Postgres add-on for vectors).
Anthropic does not sell one, so Claude Code will pick another provider's. The column size must match its output.

code.caption: user_id on every chunk is not optional. You will see why in the watch-out step.

changes: − Question, Brand Mark, Font List, Groceries, Gym Plan
+ Maya, App Server, Claude API, Database: back to Notely
+ Embedding Model: turns each chunk into a vector
~ Database: stores every chunk with its vector

scene.caption: Once, ahead of time: every note is chunked, embedded and stored.

steps.title: Step 2: find the nearest chunks
body: When Maya asks, the app server embeds her question with the same model. Now it is a point on the same map.
Then it asks Postgres for the rows whose vectors are closest. pgvector's <=> operator gives the cosine distance: smaller means more similar. Take the top five. That is retrieval.

code.code:
select note_id, content
from note_chunks
order by embedding <=> $1  -- $1 = the question's vector
limit 5;
code.caption: Sorting by distance: the five chunks closest in meaning to the question.

changes: ~ Maya asks again; her question is embedded
~ Database: returns the five closest chunks
~ Useful matches 0 → 5

scene.caption: The question becomes a vector, and the database returns its nearest neighbors.

steps.title: Step 3: answer from what you found
body: The app server puts those chunks in the prompt, tagged with note ids, and asks the model to answer only from them, cite ids, and admit when the answer is missing.
Retrieve, add to the prompt, generate: that is RAG. The model reads five paragraphs, not 2,000 notes, and each claim links to its source.

code.caption: The prompt habits from lesson 3: labeled data first, the request last, a way out.

changes: ~ Claude API: answers from five chunks and cites them
~ Prompt tokens 800 → 1,500
~ Embedding Model steps back

scene.caption: Only the best five chunks reach the model.

steps.title: Make retrieval fast and sharp
body: Without an index, Postgres compares the question with every row. An HNSW index makes nearest-match search fast on large tables, trading a little accuracy for a lot of speed.
Pure vector search can miss exact things like names or order numbers. Hybrid search combines it with Postgres's own keyword search.

code.code:
create index on note_chunks
using hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
code.caption: The operator class must match the distance you sort by: cosine here.

callout.text: You met indexes in system design. This is one more kind, built for vectors.

changes: ~ Database: gains an HNSW index for vectors
~ Claude API steps back

scene.caption: An index lets the database skip most rows when searching.

steps.title: Notely's search, scoped to Maya
body: In Supabase, wrap the search in a Postgres function and call it with supabase.rpc("match_note_chunks", …), using Maya's logged-in connection.

The function keeps only rows where user_id = auth.uid() (the logged-in user), and runs as the caller, so the RLS rules on note_chunks apply too. Two locks on one door. Lesson 4's search_notes tool calls this.

code.code:
create function match_note_chunks(
  query_embedding vector(1024),
  match_count int default 5
) returns table (note_id uuid, content text)
language sql stable security invoker
as $$
  select note_id, content from note_chunks
  where user_id = auth.uid()
  order by embedding <=> query_embedding
  limit match_count;
$$;
code.caption: security invoker: the function runs with Maya's rights, not an admin's.

callout.text: Ask: does every chunk row have a user_id, and does the search filter by it? Is it called as the user or with the service role key? What re-embeds a note when it is edited or deleted? Is there a vector index?

changes: ~ Database: search filtered to Maya's own chunks

scene.caption: The search only ever looks at Maya's rows.

steps.title: The leak: someone else's notes
body: A match function that skips the user filter, or runs with the service role key (an admin key that ignores RLS), searches every user's chunks. Leo's private note lands in Maya's prompt, and the model happily quotes it.
Once it is in the prompt, it has leaked. Filter in the database, never by asking the model to ignore things.

callout.text: Two quieter bugs. Stale: Maya edits a note, the old chunks stay, answers quote deleted text; re-embed on every change. Mixed models: vectors from two embedding models do not compare; switching means re-embedding everything.

changes: ~ Database: user filter missing, searches all users
~ Claude API: quotes another user's note

scene.caption: Without the filter, other people's notes flow into Maya's answer.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Embeddings turn meaning into points on a map, so search finds "brand mark" when you ask about the logo.

RAG has two halves. Ahead of time: chunk, embed, store in pgvector. Per question: embed it with the same model, fetch the nearest chunks for this user only, and let the model answer from them with citations. Keep the index fresh.
changes: ~ Database: filtered to Maya again
~ Claude API: answers from Maya's notes, with sources
~ Embedding Model back in view

scene.caption: Index once, retrieve per question, answer from your own data.

quiz.question: Why does vector search find the "blue brand mark" note when Maya asks about the "logo"?

options.text: Postgres knows that logo and brand mark are synonyms.
options.why: Postgres compares numbers. The meaning comes from the embedding model that produced them.

options.text: Their embeddings are close, because the texts have similar meaning.
options.why: Embedding models place related meanings near each other, even with no shared words. Nearest-match search finds them.

options.text: The chat model reads all 2,000 notes and picks the right one.
options.why: That is exactly what RAG avoids. Only the top few chunks ever reach the chat model.

quiz.question: Maya deleted a paragraph from a note last week, but the chat still quotes it. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The model memorized her note during training.
options.why: Models are not trained on your users' notes when you call the API. The text came from your own data.
Approximate search may miss a close match. It does not invent text that is no longer in the table.

options.text: Old chunks were never re-embedded or deleted when the note changed.
options.why: The chunk table is a copy. Every edit or delete must update it, or retrieval keeps serving the old version.

quiz.question: Claude Code wrote a match_note_chunks function with no user_id filter and calls it with the service role key "for speed". What do you ask for?

options.text: Filter by auth.uid() and call it with the logged-in user's connection, so RLS applies.
options.why: Without both, the nearest chunks can come from any user's notes, and then they land in Maya's answer.

options.text: Nothing, as long as the prompt tells the model to ignore other users' notes.
options.why: Once another user's text is in the prompt, it has already leaked. Filtering must happen in the database.

options.text: Add an HNSW index so the search is fast without the service role.
options.why: An index helps speed, but the issue is access. The fix is the user filter and the user's own connection.

takeaways: An embedding is meaning as numbers. Near vectors mean similar text, even with different words.
RAG = index ahead of time, retrieve the nearest chunks per question, answer only from them with citations.
In Supabase: pgvector, a vector(n) column that matches your model, an hnsw index, a match function.
Every chunk carries a user_id, and every search runs as the user, so RLS applies.
Re-embed on every edit and delete, and re-embed everything when you switch embedding models.
